drills.name: Ginga
drills.desc: Capoeira's constant base movement: a triangular back-and-forth step that keeps the body swinging, never static, with the arms guarding the face in rhythm. Every attack, escape and floreio launches from somewhere inside the ginga. It is disguise and engine at once — the game's heartbeat.
mistakes: Stepping mechanically to a count instead of flowing with the rhythm of the berimbau.
Dropping the guard arm away from the face during the sway.
Staying tall and stiff — the ginga lives in bent knees and loose hips.

drills.name: Negativa
drills.desc: Dropping low onto one bent leg with the other extended, torso close to the floor and one hand posted — denying the opponent a target while staying mobile. From negativa the capoeirista sweeps, escapes or rolls away. It teaches the floor as home, not as danger.
mistakes: Sitting the weight fully on the floor instead of staying loaded and ready to move.
Letting the extended leg go limp rather than active for a sweep.
Head down watching the floor instead of the opponent.

drills.name: Rolê
drills.desc: A low rotating transition that carries the body around its own axis on hands and feet, usually out of negativa or an esquiva, always facing the opponent. It's how capoeiristas travel across the roda without standing up into an attack. Smooth weight transfer between hands and feet is the whole skill.
mistakes: Turning the back to the opponent mid-rotation.
Standing up out of the movement instead of staying low and connected.
Collapsing through soft wrists — the arms must be structural.

drills.name: Cocorinha
drills.desc: Dropping into a full deep squat on the heels, one arm shielding the head, to let a high kick pass overhead. The simplest esquiva — but it demands the ankle and hip mobility to sit at the very bottom of a squat, balanced and relaxed. Recover into ginga or answer with a sweep.
mistakes: Rising onto the toes with heels off the floor — no balance, no base.
Ducking the head forward instead of dropping the hips straight down.
Forgetting the guarding arm above the head.

drills.name: Esquiva lateral
drills.desc: Folding the torso sideways and down over a bent front leg as a kick sweeps through where the head was, one hand posted or guarding. Esquivas are capoeira's answer instead of blocking: yield, vanish, reappear with an attack. The eyes never leave the opponent through the whole dip.
mistakes: Bending only at the waist while the legs stay straight and rooted.
Looking at the floor mid-esquiva and losing the opponent.
Escaping without a plan to counter — an esquiva should load the reply.

drills.name: Esquiva baixa
drills.desc: A deep diagonal escape: one leg lunges long while the torso folds low over the bent leg, hand posted, sliding the body entirely under a spinning kick. It's the esquiva that pairs with meia lua de compasso in the endless question-and-answer of the game. Strong hips make it an ambush position, not a retreat.
mistakes: Staying too high so the kick still clips the head or shoulder.
Collapsing onto the posted hand instead of loading the legs.
Freezing at the bottom rather than flowing into rolê or a counter.

drills.name: Meia lua de frente
drills.desc: An inside-to-outside crescent kick sweeping across the opponent's face with a straight leg. The leg swings like a pendulum from the hip while the torso counterbalances — it probes distance and forces esquivas without huge commitment. Capoeira's first kick, and its politest question.
mistakes: Bending the kicking leg and turning the crescent into a weak flick.
Kicking so hard you spin off balance out of the ginga.
Dropping both arms while the leg is in the air.

drills.name: Benção
drills.desc: A straight push kick driving the flat of the foot into the opponent's chest or hips — the 'blessing' delivered with the sole. Chamber the knee high, then extend hips and leg together, pushing through the target rather than tapping it. Often thrown as the answer when an opponent crowds the ginga.
mistakes: Slapping with the toes instead of pushing through the sole of the foot.
Skipping the knee chamber and telegraphing a slow rising kick.
Leaning so far back the kick has no forward drive.

drills.name: Queixada
drills.desc: An outside-to-inside crescent aimed at the chin ('queixo'), launched after a step-across that coils the hips. The torso twists first and the straight leg follows, whipping across the target line. Its beauty is the disguise — the preparatory step looks like simple ginga until the leg is already airborne.
mistakes: Kicking from a square stance without the crossing step that loads the hips.
Bending the leg mid-arc and losing the whip.
Landing heavy and stuck instead of flowing back into ginga.

drills.name: Armada
drills.desc: A full spinning crescent: the body rotates over the support leg, the head whips around to re-spot the target, and the straight leg arrives with all the momentum of the turn. Power comes from the coiled spin, not the leg — the kick is simply where the rotation exits. The signature kick of the roda.
mistakes: Spinning without spotting — the head must turn first to find the target.
Leaning the torso away and dumping the kick’s height.
Kicking with a bent leg so the crescent loses reach and snap.

drills.name: Martelo
drills.desc: Capoeira's roundhouse: knee chambers across, support foot pivots, and the instep snaps into ribs or head like a hammer blow. Unlike the crescents it strikes with committed hip rotation — this is the kick capoeiristas bring to crosstraining. Retract as fast as it fires to stay inside the game's flow.
mistakes: Support foot doesn’t pivot, choking the hip rotation.
Striking with the toes instead of the instep.
Leaving the leg extended after impact instead of snapping it back.

drills.name: Meia lua de compasso
drills.desc: Capoeira's most iconic strike: hands drop to the floor between the legs, the head ducks through, and the body spins like a compass while the heel scythes at head height. The grounded hands make it stable, deceptive and brutally powerful. It flows straight out of esquiva baixa, attack hidden inside defense.
mistakes: Looking at the floor instead of sighting the target between the legs.
Bending the kicking leg — the heel must travel on a long, straight arc.
Placing the hands too far from the feet, stalling the spin.

drills.name: Aú
drills.desc: The cartwheel of the roda — slower and lower than a gymnast's, elbows soft, head turned to watch the opponent throughout. The aú travels, escapes and baits, and in the game it's often thrown with bent legs ready to kick from upside down. Shoulder stability and confident wrists are its foundation.
mistakes: Throwing the legs over fast and blind instead of controlled and watching the game.
Bending at the hips so the aú becomes a low hop, not an inversion.
Fingers pointed inward, straining the wrists on landing.

drills.name: Queda de rins
drills.alt: Fall onto the kidneys — elbow balance
drills.desc: A sideways balance where the body folds onto one elbow tucked into the waist, head and hand posted, legs floating free. It's both an escape under kicks and a gateway to inverted transitions. The elbow shelf takes the weight — arm strength matters less than knowing where to stack the hips.
mistakes: Elbow floating away from the hip instead of digging into the waist as a shelf.
Holding the breath and going rigid — the balance needs relaxed adjustment.
Dropping the head instead of posting it as the third point of support.

drills.name: Bananeira
drills.desc: The capoeira handstand: held with the head up and eyes on the opponent, legs often bent or split, ready to descend into a kick or aú. Unlike gymnastics the line matters less than the awareness — it's a lookout post, not a pose. Builds the inverted confidence every floreio depends on.
mistakes: Tucking the chin to the chest and losing sight of the game.
Banana-backing with flared ribs instead of bracing the core.
Fingers passive — grip the floor and steer the balance with the fingertips.

drills.name: Macaco
drills.alt: Monkey flip — back walkover from squat
drills.desc: From a low squat, one hand reaches back to the floor and the legs explode overhead in a whipping backward rotation — part back-walkover, part flip. The macaco demands explosive hips, a mobile thoracic spine and total trust in one posting arm. Land it soft and it flows straight back into ginga.
mistakes: Reaching back timidly with no leg drive — hesitation stalls the rotation mid-air.
Throwing the head back first instead of leading with the hips.
Landing stiff-legged and jarring the knees instead of flowing out.
